title_en: The Rings of Power Season 3 Showrunners Promise That They Know What the Last Shot of the Series Will Be
summary_en: The Rings of Power Season 3 just ended, so showrunners J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay break down everything that happened - and what to expect next.
body_en:
Spoilers follow for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3.
The last frame of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 focuses on Sauron (Charlie Vickers) looking straight to camera as he bows before the crowing King Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) and the very sober-looking elves Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) and Gil-galad (Benjamin Walker). A slight smirk has never been more dangerous.
With the fourth season of The Rings of Power confirmed, series creators and showrunners J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay spoke with IGN to preview what’s coming in Season 4 and beyond. From the Galadriel/Celeborn/Sauron triangle to Queen Miriel’s (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) sacrifices that seem for naught to Gandalf’s future trials and beyond, the two break down how Middle-earth will fare in the planned last two seasons.
Payne told IGN that they settled on Sauron’s last look for the season early on, despite mulling whether they should close on the forging of the One Ring instead. “There was maybe a half a second where we said, ‘Gosh, the forging of the ring is such a climactic moment. Should we end the season there and then let all the next season be about Númenór?’” he said. “Very quickly we were like, ‘No, no, no!’ You want to actually give all the other storylines a chance to coalesce. You had Gandalf out in the east working to try to take the Dark Wizard either off the field or onto his side. And Númenór in the west are figuring out their civil war and Pharazôn and Miriel's marriage. We felt like if we ended on the forging of the ring, you would feel a little frustrated.”
McKay added that they wanted to downplay this finale after two seasons of massive, action-centric season endings. “We wanted a season that was tighter, tauter, more psychological,” he explained. “And we have this great moment from mythology – that Sauron surrendered with a plan of a longer game.
“Now, that's scary as showrunners making a show in 2026,” McKay admitted. “Are people going to be like, ‘Wait, what ?’ I think that's still scary. Reactions are just coming in right now. But we also felt that it was bold, and we hadn't seen it before. When we were really [story-]beating out the very ending of the season, Sauron falls to his knees in front of the army — that image felt so strong. We were just like, ‘Let's stop right there and leave them hanging.’ It felt like a satisfying ending.”
A huge event in the Second Age of Middle-earth is the Fall of Númenór to Sauron, and McKay and Payne confirm that that train is now on the tracks.
“It’s a real opportunity to show a civilizational decline,” Payne said of what’s to come. “Fall is one of Tolkien's recurring themes [that] he goes back to again and again. We've already seen the cracks in Númenór. We know they're there, so how do you exploit those to get the mightiest empire of men that has ever existed and totally take them off the map?”
Without spoiling, Payne said they’re very excited to show it in a “multifaceted way,” along with its effect on many different characters and storylines. But there’s also the interpersonal drama to come between Pharazôn and Sauron. In prior seasons, audiences have already seen the Dark Lord pick apart Galadriel and others, so how will Pharazôn be undone?
“Pharazôn is a very skilled and savvy manipulator in his own right,” Payne said of the King. “He's a massive politician. He's one who is always looking seven moves down the chessboard and trying to figure out how to outsmart his adversary. When you get two snakes in a barrel, each one trying to outmaneuver the other one and look ahead, how is Sauron able to concoct a lose-lose scenario that even someone as savvy as Pharazôn might fall prey to?”
McKay was also gleeful about it. “The idea of putting Charlie Vickers and Trystan Gravelle on a collision course — that's a potent mix. Those are two very exciting actors with very different approaches, playing very different kinds of characters. We're pretty excited.”
Also in that Númenórean psychological soup is the sacrificial Queen Miriel, who only married Pharazôn to join his army with her Faithful in order to bring down Sauron. And now the Dark Lord is coming home with them?
“It is a terrible compromise she has made, but one that she believes is the best given everything on her plate,” McKay pointed out. “She's trying to save her people and save the world, and she's sacrificing herself in the process. Now extrapolate – what does that person do when Sauron's here with the influence he's having? There's two things that person could do. They could continue doubling down and trying to fix it, digging the hole even deeper to protect her people. Or she could say, ‘I'm out.’ I think if you look at Cynthia's amazing performance and the journey this character has been on, it's going to be a rough road ahead for the Queen. The Queen has a big story next season. Everyone in Númenór does.”
In Season 1, Sauron/Halbrand really created a connection with Galadriel, and his betrayal has continued to pull on both of them through Season 3. With the return of the long-lost Celeborn this season, a choice was made. In the finale, the married elves chose one another, but Sauron was clearly looking right at Galadriel when he took the knee for Pharazôn.
McKay said it was their intention to tell a real, messy love story this season with Galadriel and Celeborn, with an eye to countering Sauron’s quest to forge the ring. “When [Galadriel and Celeborn] see each other, on the one hand, they're both in tears. But also, it's like, ‘What does this mean?’ They're unmoored. It breaks their reality.
“By the end of the season, they have renegotiated their marriage and found a place where they can be equals … both of them have been traumatized by the Dark Lord,” McKay points out. “That also means that that core relationship and the dream they had of the realm and bringing light and beauty into the world – they're going to fight and try to protect that ever more fiercely now that they really know the stakes of it.”
As for Sauron, Payne said that there are many prices he must pay for his mission to take Middle-earth, including how he feels about Galadriel. “We know that this is going to be a connection that endures into the Third Age,” he said of Tolkien’s lore. “Galadriel tells us that she knows the Dark Lord and his mind, and that ever does he grope after her to know hers. So Sauron is never letting this go. But she says, ‘Still the way is shut.’ She has closed that door, and now we're going to watch as she figures out a way to heal from the damage that it has done to her. And Celeborn finds a way to heal from the damage that it has also done to him.”
McKay said how they will achieve that ties to Pharazôn asking for their counsel about how to get at Sauron before the battle that never happened. “That speaks to the role of Galadriel and Celeborn moving forward, which is — they know this guy,” he pointed out. “They know him better than anyone, which makes them natural adversaries for him, so that will come back around as well.”
What about the fledgling wizard who succeeded in helping the Dark Wizard / Pallando (Ciarán Hinds) redeem his evil ways? Gandalf has his staff and his hat, and that huge win under his belt. Who does he help next?
Payne teased that Gandalf’s work is far from done, and instead of turning one heart, he’s going to have to figure out how to turn the “hearts of entire people and leaders.”
“What are the challenges that come together when he has to get people who are enemies, or deep enemies, to put aside differences [and] come together?” Payne posed. “What sacrifices will he have to make? These are all things that are still down the road for Gandalf.”
McKay said they are now in the phase of shaping this series where they’re dovetailing back into the concrete canon of Tolkien’s books, and adaptation going forward will be more precise.
“From the very beginning when we first started our first writers' room, it was about charting those giant moments,” he explained. “In some ways, the making of the three rings was the end of the first season. The seven and the nine [rings were] in the second [season]. And this season was all about the One Ring, ending in [Sauron’s] surrender. And there's a very clear plan for the rest. We know where we're heading.
“We even know what the last shot is,” he revealed. “There is some problem-solving we have yet to do, like how much of this? Or, how are we going to do that? But the garden of forking paths is narrow ahead. We know what we're doing next [season], and I think we have a pretty good idea what we're going to do the time after that. It does feel like we're over the hump, and it does feel like the destination is in sight.”
